description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

In this section (maximum 1000 words), please provide a global overview of the project progress **per output**. To what extent have they been achieved? Comment on the activities that have taken place and the most important milestones.

actual.value:
Phase 1 of the implementation concerned an in-depth analysis of the AAH South Sudan team and the target community. We conducted multiple surveys to gather information on: • From AAH-SS: understanding of entrepreneurship/business concepts, the level of skills and capacity as trainers and program managers, their support needs. • From target community: the profiles of the potential entrepreneurship participants, the economic sectors in the community, the hurdles faced (by men v women), their support needs. The research among AAH-SS staff was conducted through 1-on-1 interviews by CWW. In total we managed to conduct 5 interviews with over 8 AAH-SS staff and AAH-I staff. The research among the target community was set-up by CWW, but conducted by AAH staff, given the language barrier - the common tongue in their communities is Juba Arabic. We created survey’s to be filled out by the staff who liaise with the local communities. The understanding that we received from the research was that the literacy level was practically non-existent and the communities, our target audience don’t live in villages in close knit groups but are semi-nomadic where they roam the rural areas of South Sudan in the drought and settle during the wet season, mainly on the banks of the river. During this wet season, businesses would spring up and those that had any starting capital could invest in products to sell. Tea shops, small bakeries, phone charging stalls seemed to be the most common types of businesses that would serve as our target audience.
This research informed the 2 elements of the training that CWW and AAHI have developed: the management training and the curriculum training. We created the in person training week to encompass: A 8 to 12 lesson interactive entrepreneurship curriculum for AAH-SS to use in their communities. This curriculum includes presentations, trainer manuals, participant workbooks and everything else needed for AAH-SS to conduct the curriculum. CWW and AAHI have provide training-of-trainers sessions to AAH South Sudan to master this curriculum. A 3 to 5 lesson Management program for AAH-SS staff to become effective program managers and trainers of entrepreneurship programs.
Post training in Nairobi, the curriculum was shared with the AAH-SS staff to be translated into Sudanese Arabic. Right after, a sourcing plan was made to start sourcing the types of cooperatives that could join the ‘Jumpstart’ Programme. However, plans were disrupted with insecurity incidents that resulted from cattle invasion from our project areas of Eastern Equatoria state, the environment couldn't enable conduct of trainings. After closely monitoring the security situation, training was resumed after a small delay. Currently, at project end, we have successfully managed to conduct all required trainings with the cohorts of agri-entrepreneurs and cooperatives in Eastern Equatoria state.
